activities.anchor: picture the studio as a chain of translators
activities.caption: rebuild the chain from voice to file
activities.name: rfChainOrder

config.prompt: A voice makes pressure waves; a file stores numbers. Order the translators between them:
items: The source — voice or drum, an acoustic event with its own spectrum and dynamics
Microphone — a diaphragm turns pressure waves into a tiny electrical voltage
Preamp — raises that voltage to a workable level
Converter — turns the voltage into numbers a computer can store
Recorder — writes the numbers to a file
config.why: At every link two enemies wait: noise rising from below and distortion dropping from above — the craft is getting the music between them, every time, on every take.

activities.caption: you hear the clip — decide what happens next
activities.name: rfClipBranch

config.root: Listen-back: the loudest chorus of the vocal take is clipped at the converter — 0 dBFS sliced the waveform's tips.

start.text: The take is musically the best one. What do you do?

choices.label: Open a de-clipper plugin and repair the waveform
choices.feedback: Editing and mixing reshape what was captured — the clipped tips were never recorded, so the repair is guessing.

choices.label: Re-track the vocal with more headroom before the next pass
choices.feedback: Decisions made before pressing record are worth more than any correction applied after.

repair.text: A de-clipper can guess at the missing tips, but the cause is baked in: a badly recorded source is a permanent tax. The professional move is re-tracking.

retrack.text: Lower the preamp gain for the next pass, leave headroom at performance level, and the take survives every future mix — capture, don't rescue.

config.why: Editing, tuning and mixing only reshape what exists — a vocal clipped at the converter cannot be un-clipped, and a roomy thin guitar sound cannot lose its room.

activities.anchor: work like a tiny loudspeaker in reverse
activities.caption: drag the divider — the two great microphone families
activities.name: rfMicCompare

config.prompt: Dynamic or condenser? Drag the divider between the two families:

before.label: Dynamic
before.text: Rugged, cheap-ish, tolerant of brutal sound-pressure levels and awkward rooms — the SM57/SM58 family lives on guitar amplifiers, snare drums and stages.

after.label: Condenser
after.text: Far finer detail and sensitivity — the default studio vocal mic — but it needs +48 V phantom power down the cable, hears everything (bad rooms, computer fans) and overloads in front of a kick drum.

config.why: Choose for source and room, not price — the choice depends on what you record and where.

activities.anchor: Placement is the cheaper and mightier tool
activities.caption: file each move under the lever that does the work
activities.name: rfLeverBuckets

config.prompt: Three levers move the mic before EQ does. File each effect:

items.label: 2–5 cm from the lips: almost all direct sound, intimate and dry
pulled back to 30 cm: the mic breathes with the room
directional mics boost bass as they get closer (proximity effect)
two mics on one source spaced too close: the delay between them comb-filters the blend

config.why: Experienced engineers change the mic's position before reaching for EQ — placement is the first EQ.

activities.anchor: A worked case: recording a guitar amplifier
activities.caption: pair each mic position with the tone it returns
activities.name: rfAmpMatch

config.prompt: One SM57, one amp, four moves. Pair position with result:

pairs.left: where the cone meets the dust cap
pairs.right: bright and present — the standard move

config.why: Move the mic through those positions while the player repeats a loop, listening for the one where the tone is right at the source — because at the source, correction is free.

activities.caption: true or false — price versus position
activities.name: rfPriceJudge

statements.s: A well-placed SM57 in a good position beats a boutique condenser badly placed.
statements.why: Placement and the room dominate price in almost every practical test.
It buys detail, consistency, lower self-noise — real, but the last few percent.

statements.s: The microphone is the first fifty percent; the position is the last few.
statements.why: Inverted — the position is the first fifty; the microphone is the last few percent.

statements.s: A bad room defeats an expensive microphone.
statements.why: Condensers hear everything, including bad rooms — and the room is on every recording.

activities.anchor: is the map of a studio
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the discipline and its two bookends
activities.name: rfGainCloze

config.text: %%0%% is the discipline of setting each stage's level so the signal stays far above the %%1%% below and far below the %%2%% above at every link.
config.hint: One is the discipline; the other two are the enemies waiting at every link.

activities.anchor: record as hot as possible like the tape era taught
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the tape-era habit
activities.name: rfHotSpot

config.prompt: A producer's plan for tracking the album contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Set gain during a confident rehearsal pass at performance level.
Tape saturated gracefully — pushing levels added a pleasing compression.
Digital saturates the same way, so hot levels flatter the file too.
Modern practice records conservatively and adds character in the mix on purpose.
config.correction: Digital has no sweet spot at the top — 0 dBFS is a cliff, not a colour; the same habit that flattered tape writes irreversible distortion into a file.
config.why: Tape flattered hot levels; the converter slices them — record conservatively, then lift the quiet, healthy file later.
